title: A Triumph for All: Gosnell and the Nisga'a Treaty
intro: A 1998 speech closes a century-long struggle. Begin Assignment 2.1 here; you write it after Lesson 2.

terms.def: The formal assertion of Aboriginal title or other rights to a territory, negotiated or litigated toward settlement.
Care of the land as an obligation: use and sharing within need, never ownership for its own sake.

body: In 1998, Nisga'a leader Dr. Joseph Gosnell rose in the British Columbia Legislature to mark the end of a struggle more than a century old. The Nisga'a had first petitioned governments to recognize their land rights generations earlier; now the Nisga'a Treaty would make them, in his words, no longer wards of the state and no longer beggars in their own lands.

Gosnell called the treaty a triumph for all British Columbians, and a beacon of hope for Aboriginal people worldwide. Under it the Nisga'a would collectively own about 2,000 square kilometres, far beyond the postage-stamp reserves of colonial governments, govern themselves through their own institutions within Canadian law, and be free, in his phrase, to make their own mistakes and savour their own victories.

To Gosnell a treaty is a sacred instrument, the legal framework for a new society. That claim sets the chapter's work: why land claims matter to Aboriginal groups, how different peoples value land, what kinds of claims the federal government recognizes, how claims get resolved, and how self-government connects to land. Notice the last focus question too, because perspectives on Aboriginal land rights have shifted enormously over time, and they keep shifting.

Through land claims, Aboriginal peoples assert their rights as the continent's Indigenous peoples, and through land they secure their cultures' future. This theme follows the chapter's arc from values to history to process to conflict to settlement, and Assignment 2.1 starts now: it asks what oral tradition teaches about stewardship versus the non-Native idea of ownership, so bank one stewardship example from Theme 1's first lesson and one from this theme as you read.

example.title: Assignment 2.1 starts here
example.text: Assignment 2.1 asks what oral tradition teaches about stewardship versus the non-Native idea of ownership. Collect one stewardship example from Lesson 1 of Theme 1 and one from Lesson 2 of this theme now; you write the paragraph after Lesson 2.

check.prompt: Gosnell called the treaty a triumph for all British Columbians, not only for the Nisga'a. Why?
check.sample: Sample response: it ended wardship and brought the Nisga'a in as full, equal participants in the province's life, while showing the world that a negotiated treaty can replace a century of denial.

title: Six Ways to Value Land
intro: Economic, cultural, spiritual, educational, social, and political value, through two worldviews.

terms.def: Full private ownership of land that can be bought, sold, or borrowed against on the open market.
Using land and its resources so the way of life and the community they support can continue.

body: In the non-Aboriginal worldview the loudest value is economic: what land or its resources can be bought or sold for, quantified in dollars, unlocked by owning land in fee simple and usable as security for loans. From an Aboriginal worldview land is economically valuable too, but as a living to be made, in traditional and non-traditional ways, hunting, fishing, and trapping that all depend on a land base and access to unoccupied Crown lands.

The deeper difference is the end goal. Seneca Elder Twylah Hurd Nitsch calls land a shared, living entity, and the chapter insists traditional Aboriginal people would no more destroy the land than themselves: the goal is maintaining a way of life and a community, not maximizing a return. That does not rule out revenue. Forestry, energy, minerals, agriculture, and tourism all prosper on Aboriginal land, from the Nakoda First Nation's mountain lodge to Roland Woodward's demand that his Treaty 8 people control the surface and subsurface rights beneath the Athabasca oil, gas, and timber.

Then come the values no market prices. Cultural value roots identity in a homeland; spiritual value treats the land as kin rather than commodity; educational value makes the land itself the classroom where Elders teach history, law, and proper behaviour. These are why the chapter keeps returning to oral tradition: the stories are the curriculum, and without the land they describe, the teaching thins.

Social and political value complete the six: land holds a community together and underwrites its right to govern itself. Perspectives on all six differ between cultures and change across a lifetime, which is the point of the talking-circle activity and the profile of Launa Loyie. For Assignment 2.1, this lesson is your Theme 2 evidence bank: every value above is stewardship in action, set against ownership as domination.

example.title: Worked contrast
example.text: Take one forest. Through fee simple it is timber revenue minus costs. Through stewardship it is also a classroom, a pharmacy, a hunting ground, and an ancestor's instruction. Assignment 2.1 wants exactly this double vision in one paragraph.

check.prompt: Give one economic argument about the same land from each worldview.
check.sample: Sample response: fee-simple view: sell the timber and invest the proceeds. Stewardship view: harvest within need so hunting, teaching, and community life on that land can continue, and reinvest resource income in the community.

title: From Petitions to Policy: The Calder Case
intro: Royal Proclamation roots, a century of denial, and the court case that forced a claims policy.

terms.def: A claim over territory where Aboriginal title was never ceded by treaty, proven through research and negotiated toward agreement.
A claim that the Crown failed to keep a treaty promise, such as a reserve that was never surveyed.

body: The roots run to the Royal Proclamation of 1763, which recognized Aboriginal title and gave the Crown alone the right to negotiate its extinguishment. Over the next century and a half the Crown signed treaties across much of the country, promising reserves, payments, schooling, and continued traditional use. But large areas and many peoples were left out entirely: no Métis or Inuit group signed any treaty, and some First Nations never did either.

British Columbia denied even harder. When it joined Confederation in 1871, Ottawa planned prairie-style treaties, but Lieutenant-Governor Joseph Trutch did not believe First Nations held land rights at all. Against that wall the Nisga'a organized: a 1913 petition that stands as Canada's first land claim, then, after 1951 Indian Act revisions let First Nations organize again, a re-established land committee under the Nisga'a Tribal Council.

In 1967 that council, led by Dr. Frank Calder, took the title question to the Supreme Court of Canada. The court split, could not agree on the claim itself, and rejected it on a technicality, but its ruling declared that where the Crown never explicitly extinguished title, Aboriginal peoples could still hold rights to land and resources. Title, in other words, legally pre-existed any Crown declaration of sovereignty.

Calder cracked a century of denial open and forced Ottawa to build a claims policy with two doors. A comprehensive claim covers ground no treaty ever touched, proven by research into use and occupancy since time immemorial. A specific claim alleges a broken treaty promise. Assignment 2.2 starts here: you will profile two Alberta claims, so from this lesson on, sort every file you meet by asking first whether any treaty covers the ground.

example.title: Worked sorting
example.text: Ask first: was title ceded here? If no treaty covers the ground, the file runs comprehensive. If a treaty promised a reserve that never arrived, the file runs specific. Keep a running list; Lesson 5 hands you Bigstone Cree as your first worked file.

check.prompt: The Nisga'a lost the Calder case on a technicality. Why did they still win the larger point?
check.sample: Sample response: the court declared that Aboriginal title survives unless the Crown explicitly extinguished it, so title pre-exists Crown sovereignty claims, and Ottawa had to create a real claims policy.
